newsitem.title: INDIA: India wants talks with Pakistan but not on Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: India wants talks with Pakistan but not on Kashmir.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said on Thursday he favoured the resumption of peace talks with Pakistan but that New Delhi would never give up the area of Kashmir it controls.
Deve Gowda told troops in Kashmir that he would send Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral to Pakistan for talks if Islamabad extended an invitation.

"As soon as I receive the invitation, I will ask the external affairs minister to go to Pakistan for talks," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Deve Gowda as saying. "We want to improve our relations with Islamabad."
Later Deve Gowda told a public meeting in the winter capital of Jammu and Kashmir state that he hoped ministerial-level talks would soon be held with Pakistan.
But he cautioned Islamabad not to expect to negotiate over the two thirds of Kashmir which is part of Jammu and Kashmir.
"So far as the Kashmir issue is concerned, it is a closed chapter," Deve Gowda said. "Jammu and Kashmir is a part and parcel of India, and there is no question of its compromise."
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
Pakistan, which rules over one third of Kashmir, has long insisted the two sides resolve their differences over the mountainous region before taking up other bilateral issues.
But New Delhi has rejected Islamabads insistence that an internationally supervised plebiscite be held in Kashmir to determine the regions future status.

India accuses Pakistan of arming and training militants fighting New Delhis rule in Jammu and Kashmir, where more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since a separatist rebellion erupted in 1990. Islamabad says it provides the guerrillas only diplomatic and moral support.
Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah recently drew heated criticism from nationalists when he suggested that the line of control dividing Kashmir be made a final boundary.
The opposition Bharatiya Janata Party accused Abdullah of proposing that India relinquish its claim over the area of Kashmir ruled by Pakistan.
Deve Gowda recalled Pakistani prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharifs recent statement offering dialogue to usher in a new era in relations between the longtime foes.
"Mr Sharifs initial views have been favourable and I hope that the new government in Pakistan will show a positive approach in this regard," PTI quoted Deve Gowda as saying.

Deve Gowda and ousted Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto exchanged letters after the Indian prime minister took office last June, but the notes did not lead to high-level bilateral talks, which were last held in January 1994.
Sharifs overwhelming victory in Pakistans polls earlier this month has raised hopes that peace talks could be resumed.

During his tightly guarded visit to the northern state, Deve Gowda inaugurated a 480-megawatt hydroelectric plant in Uri and promised 75 billion rupees ($2.1 billion) in federal economic aid to the state.
